title: Range-based for
learningGoals: loop over every item with a range-based for
loop over the letters of a string

youtube.title: C++ Range-Based for Loop | C++ Programming EP 18
youtube.description: In this episode you will loop over every item with a range-based for, loop over the letters of a string and change items with a reference, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Range-based for · 0:52 Visit every item · 1:32 Round by round · 2:02 Second program · 3:02 Recap · 3:32 Bug of the Day · 4:20 Challenge · 4:40 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "FOR EACH" in tomato on cream; Xecxec next to a crab picking up one shell at a time; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a crab picking up one shell at a time

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we loop without a counter. The range-based for visits every item for you, one at a time.

scenes.onScreen: "Range-based for": numbered lines (1. Range-based for visits every item; 2. No counter is needed; 3. An ampersand lets you change the items) and an analogy card: a teacher calling the roll: each name is called once, in order
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A range-based for loop visits every item in a group. You do not need a counter, and you cannot go past the end. It works on strings, lists and many other groups. By default the loop variable is a copy. Add an ampersand to work on the real item. Think of a teacher calling the roll. Each name is called once, in order.
points: An ampersand lets you change the items

analogy.title: Range-based for
analogy.body: A teacher calling the roll: each name is called once, in order

scenes.onScreen: foreach.cpp: a range-based for over letters and numbers
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 6] Word holds Goa. [HL 7] The loop takes each letter in turn and puts it in c. [TRACK c=G] First c is G. [TRACK c=o] Then o. [TRACK c=a] Then a. [HL 10] This loop visits the numbers ten, twenty and thirty. [HL 11] It prints each one.

scenes.onScreen: a table: round, the item and the action
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Here is the loop over Goa. In each round, the loop gives us the next letter. After the last letter, no items remain. The loop ends by itself. You never write a test or a step.

diagram.caption: a table: round, the item and the action

scenes.onScreen: vowels.cpp: a range-based for counts vowels in a word
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] Word holds Konkani. [HL 7] The count starts at zero. [HL 8] The loop visits each letter. [HL 9] An if tests the letter against five vowels. [HL 10] A vowel adds one to the count. [TRACK vowels=3] The word Konkani has three vowels, which are o, a and i. [HL 13] The program prints the count.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as vowels dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints Vowels colon three.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A range-based for visits every item. Two. You need no counter and no test. Three. By default the loop variable is a copy. Four. Add an ampersand to change the real item. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A range-based for visits every item.
You need no counter and no test.
By default the loop variable is a copy.
Add an ampersand to change the real item.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Changing a copy
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We try to change goa into capital letters. But the program prints goa again. The loop variable c is a copy. We change the copy and not the string. Add an ampersand after char. Then c is a nickname for the real letter.

scenes.onScreen: I wrote a for-each loop for my fish. Now every fish gets visited exactly once.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I wrote a for-each loop for my fish. Now every fish gets visited exactly once.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: count the letter a
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Read a word. Use a range-based for to count how many times the letter a appears. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: break and continue. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

goa
bug.why: Without the ampersand, c is a copy of each letter. The code changes the copy, and the real string stays the same.

pun: "I wrote a for-each loop for my fish. Now every fish gets visited exactly once."
challenge: Read a word. Use a range-based for to count how many times the letter a appears.
challengeAnswer: Read the word into a string. Loop over each char. If the char is the letter a, add one to a counter.
